summary: Proposes a revised model of who may sign what in DNSSEC, aiming to clarify earlier documents and add restrictions that make secure resolution simpler. In particular it affects which keys are allowed to sign which sets of records. It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC tightens one rule in DNSSEC. Earlier documents allowed a host or a user key to sign a zone's data and have the signature count. This RFC says only the zone's own key may do that, and lists the checks a resolver has to run before it trusts any signature.

questions: which keys can sign dns records
what are zone keys in dnssec
subtitle: A tighter rule for which DNSSEC keys count as authorized to sign DNS data.

tldr.problem: Earlier DNSSEC documents let a host key or a user key sign data in a way that counted for DNSSEC validation, which left a resolver with a complicated judgement to make about whether a key had the authority to sign what it had signed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tightens the rule so that in a secure zone only a zone key may produce a material signature, and it lists the checks a resolver must apply to each field of a SIG record and of the KEY record that produced it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3008 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, and updated by RFC 3658.

sections.title: A Revised Model of Signing Authority
sections.content:
The RFC defines additional restrictions on DNSSEC signature records relating to their authority to sign associated data. The intent is to establish a standard policy followed by a secure resolver, and this policy can be augmented by local rules. It builds on RFC 2535, updating section 2.3.6 of that document.

The most significant change is stated up front: in a secure zone, zone data is required to be signed by the zone key. Familiarity with the DNS system and the DNS security extensions is assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule being changed is narrow but important. In a signed zone, the key that signs the data has to be the zone's own key.

sections.title: Data SIGs, SIG(0)s and Materiality
sections.content:
A SIG record is normally associated with an RRset, and "covers" that RRset, meaning it demonstrates the authenticity and integrity of the RRset. This is referred to as a data SIG. There can be multiple SIG records covering an RRset, and the same validation process should be repeated for each of them.

Some data SIGs are considered material, that is, relevant to a DNSSEC capable resolver, and some are immaterial or extra-DNSSEC, because they are not relevant to DNSSEC validation. Immaterial SIGs may have application defined roles. SIG records may also exist which are not bound to any RRset; these are also considered immaterial. The validation process determines which SIGs are material, and once a SIG is shown to be immaterial no other validation is necessary.

SIGs may also be used for transaction security. In that case a SIG record with a type covered field of 0 is attached to a message and is used to protect message integrity. This is referred to as a SIG(0).

The document then sets the ground rules for validation. The following sections define requirements for all of the fields of a SIG record, and these requirements must be met in order for a DNSSEC capable resolver to process the signature. If any of them are not met, the SIG cannot be further processed. Additionally, once a KEY has been identified as having generated the SIG, there are requirements that it must meet.
sections.plainLanguage: Some signatures matter to DNSSEC and some do not. A signature that protects a DNS transaction is a different kind from one that protects a set of records, and each has its own rules.

sections.title: Requirements on the SIG Record Fields
sections.content:
The RFC states the requirements field by field.

The Type Covered for a data SIG must be the same as the type of data in the associated RRset; for a SIG(0) it must be 0. The Algorithm Number specified in a SIG must be recognized by the client, and must be an algorithm that has a defined SIG rdata format. The Labels count must be less than or equal to the number of labels in the SIG owner name. The Original TTL must be greater than or equal to the TTL of the SIG record itself, since the TTL cannot be increased by intermediate servers; this field can be ignored for SIG(0) records.

The current time at the time of validation must lie within the validity period bounded by the Signature Expiration and Inception times. There are no restrictions on the Key Tag field, although future algorithms might impose constraints.

The Signer's Name field of a data SIG must contain the name of the zone to which the data and signature belong. The combination of signer's name, key tag and algorithm must identify a zone key if the SIG is to be considered material. The only exception is that the signer's name field in a SIG KEY at a zone apex should contain the parent zone's name, unless the KEY set is self-signed. There are no restrictions on the signer field of a SIG(0) record, but the combination of signer's name, key tag and algorithm must identify a key if the SIG(0) is to be processed. Finally, there are no restrictions on the Signature field; it will be verified at some point, and does not need to be examined before verification unless a future algorithm imposes constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a resolver checks the cryptography, it checks the labels on the signature: does it say it covers the right kind of record, is it still inside its validity window, and does it name the right zone?

sections.title: Requirements on the Signing KEY Record
sections.content:
Once a signature has been examined and its fields validated, but before the signature has been verified, the resolver attempts to locate a KEY that matches the signer name, key tag and algorithm fields in the SIG. If none is found, the SIG cannot be verified and is considered immaterial. If KEYs are found, several fields of the KEY record must have specific values for the SIG to be considered material and authorized. If there are multiple KEYs, the checks are performed on all of them, because there is no way to determine which one generated the signature until the verification is performed.

The Type Flags of the signing KEY record must have a value of 00 or 01, that is authentication allowed with confidentiality optional, and a DNSSEC resolver must only trust signatures generated by keys that are permitted to authenticate data.

The Name Flags are treated differently for the two kinds of signature. For a data SIG, if the SIG record covers an RRset, the name type of the associated KEY must be 01, that is zone, and the DNSSEC validation process performed by a resolver must ignore all keys that are not zone keys unless local policy dictates otherwise. The RFC explains why. RFC 2535 allowed host and user keys to generate material DNSSEC signatures in order to allow dynamic update without online zone keys, that is, to avoid storing private keys in an online server. That goal cannot be achieved anyway, because online zone keys are necessary to sign NXT and SOA sets, and these online zone keys can sign any incoming data. Removing the goal of having no online keys removes the reason to allow host and user keys to generate material signatures. Limiting material signatures to zone keys simplifies validation, because the length of the verification chain is bounded by the name's label depth and the authority of a key is clearly defined, so a resolver does not have to make a potentially complicated decision about whether a key has the proper authority to sign data.

For a SIG(0), the name type of the associated KEY should be 00, user, or 10, host or entity. Transactions are initiated by a host or a user, not by a zone, so zone keys should not generate SIG(0) records. A client is either explicitly executed by a user or on behalf of a host, so the name type of a SIG(0) generated by a client should be either user or host. A nameserver is associated with a host, and its use of SIG(0) is not associated with a particular zone, so the name type of a SIG(0) generated by a nameserver should be host.

The Signatory Flags are not assigned any values by this document, and no values are required to be present. The Protocol of the signing KEY record must have a value of 3, meaning DNSSEC, or 255, meaning ALL. If a key is not specified for use with DNSSEC, a DNSSEC resolver must not trust any signature it generates. Finally, the Algorithm Number in the KEY record must be identical to that of the generated SIG record, and must meet all the requirements for an algorithm value in a SIG record.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the zone's own key counts for zone data. A signature that protects a message is different: there the key belongs to a user or a host, because a message is sent by a person or a machine, not by a zone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC defines a standard baseline for a DNSSEC capable resolver, and says this is necessary for a thorough security analysis of DNSSEC, if one is to be done. Specifically, it places additional restrictions on the SIG records that a resolver must validate before the signature can be considered worthy of DNSSEC trust. The document says this simplifies the protocol, making it more robust and able to withstand scrutiny by the security community.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixing the rules in one place is what makes it possible to reason about whether a resolver is safe at all.

viz.caption: THE FIELD CHECKS A RESOLVER MAKES

items.title: Type covered
items.text: For a data SIG, the same as the type of the records it covers; for a SIG(0), the value 0.

items.title: Labels
items.text: No more than the number of labels in the name the signature sits under.

items.title: Original TTL
items.text: At least the TTL of the SIG record itself, since a TTL cannot be raised in transit.

items.title: Validity period
items.text: The current time must fall between the inception and expiration times.

items.title: Signer's name
items.text: For a data SIG it must be the name of the zone the data and signature belong to.
